title: Implement AI Identification and Authentication Strategies
intro: Identity for AI systems, where most identities are not people: classifying human and non-human identities, including agents; identity architectures that give non-repudiation and verified accountability through delegation, bound tokens and signed actions; machine-to-machine authentication and API tokens; federated identity, single sign-on and phishing-resistant MFA; and secrets and key management for AI platforms.
objectives: Classify human, workload, agent, tool and external identities, and apply the right ownership and authentication to each
Design identity architectures that provide non-repudiation, using delegation rather than impersonation, bound tokens, signatures and tamper-evident logs
Choose machine-to-machine authentication, preferring workload identity federation, and handle API tokens safely
Federate AI tools through single sign-on and SCIM, and apply phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access and step-up authentication
Manage secrets for AI platforms with vaults, runtime injection, credential brokering for agents, scanning and fast revocation

sections.title: Human and non-human identities in AI systems

scenes.title: Who, or what, is calling?
scenes.say: In an AI system, most identities aren’t people. Training jobs, pipelines, inference services, agents and tools call each other constantly, and each one needs an identity that can be authenticated and held to account. | This video covers how to classify identities in AI systems, and why agents need a category of their own.

scenes.title: Identity types in AI systems

items.d: Act autonomously, often for a user

scenes.say: AI systems involve six broad kinds of identity. | Human users: staff and customers who use AI applications. | Privileged humans: machine learning engineers and platform administrators, whose access to models, data and pipelines is powerful. | Workloads and services: training jobs, data pipelines and inference services. | AI agents, which act autonomously, often on behalf of a particular user. | Tools and MCP servers: the APIs that agents call. | And external AI services, such as model providers and partner organisations’ agents.

scenes.title: Human and non-human identities
rows: Joiner, mover, leaver, driven by HR
scenes.say: Human and non-human identities differ in important ways. | People authenticate with passkeys, multi-factor authentication and single sign-on. Non-human identities use certificates, tokens and workload identity. | Human lifecycles are driven by HR: joiners, movers and leavers. Non-human identities are created by code, and are often left behind when projects end. | You know your headcount, but non-human identities often outnumber people many times over. | And their typical weaknesses differ: phishing and password reuse for people; long-lived secrets and excessive privileges for machines.

scenes.title: Why agents need their own category
scenes.say: Agents don’t fit neatly into either group. | Unlike a normal workload, an agent decides what to do at run time, so its behaviour isn’t fixed in code. | It usually acts on behalf of a person, so the delegation must be recorded. | Agents multiply: they can be spawned for each task, and may live only for minutes. | They can be manipulated by the content they read. | And every action needs clear attribution: which agent, acting for whom, under which instructions. That is why agents should get their own identities, never a shared service account or a borrowed human login.

scenes.title: From discovery to a governed identity
scenes.say: Bringing identities under control follows a simple path. First, discover them: user accounts, service accounts, API keys, tokens and agents, across clouds and AI platforms. | Classify each one: human, workload, agent or tool. | Assign an accountable owner, because every non-human identity needs a person responsible for it. | Rate its risk, based on privilege, the data it can reach, and how autonomously it acts. | Choose the strongest authentication that fits: phishing-resistant MFA for people, and workload identity rather than static keys for machines. | And record it in the identity inventory, which Module 4.7 covers in detail.

items: Six kinds: users, privileged humans, workloads, agents, tools, external services
Non-human identities outnumber people and are often orphaned
Agents decide, delegate, multiply and can be manipulated
Discover, classify, own, rate, authenticate, record
scenes.say: To recap. | AI systems involve human users, privileged humans, workloads, agents, tools and external services. | Non-human identities usually outnumber people, and are often left without an owner. | Agents need their own category, because they decide at run time, act for others, multiply and can be manipulated. | And every identity should be discovered, classified, owned, risk-rated, strongly authenticated and recorded.

blocks.md:
### A classification scheme
| Category | Examples | Preferred authentication | Accountable owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Human users** | Employees, contractors, customers | SSO with phishing-resistant MFA; passkeys for customers | The person, under HR or customer terms |
| **Privileged humans** | ML engineers, platform and data administrators | Phishing-resistant MFA, privileged access management, just-in-time elevation | The person and their manager |
| **Workloads and services** | Training jobs, data pipelines, CI runners, inference services | Workload identity (platform-issued, short-lived), mTLS | The owning team |
| **AI agents** | Assistants that call tools; autonomous task agents; sub-agents | A distinct identity per agent, plus delegated tokens that record the user it acts for | A named sponsor or owner |
| **Tools and MCP servers** | Internal APIs, connectors, plugins | OAuth resource server with audience-bound tokens; mTLS | The team that operates the tool |
| **External AI services** | Model provider APIs, partner agents | Federated or OAuth credentials with scoped access; API keys only where unavoidable | The relationship owner (Module 2.5) |

### Why non-human identities need attention
Non-human identities commonly outnumber human ones many times over, and they are created by scripts, pipelines and developers rather than by HR processes. The **OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025)** highlights risks such as improper offboarding, secret leakage, over-privileged identities, long-lived secrets, reuse of one identity across systems, and humans logging in with machine identities.

### Agent identity principles
- **One identity per agent**, never a shared service account and never a human’s credentials. This makes actions attributable and lets you revoke one agent without affecting others.
- **Record delegation:** when an agent acts for a user, its tokens should show both identities (Section 2), and its rights should never exceed that user’s (Module 4.6).
- **Link to a sponsor:** every agent has a human owner responsible for its purpose, permissions and retirement.
- **Bind to configuration:** record which model version, system prompt and tools an agent identity runs with, because its behaviour depends on them.
- **Short-lived where possible:** task-scoped agents get credentials that expire with the task.

### Common mistakes
- Agents running under a developer’s personal account or API key.
- One shared "AI service account" used by every assistant and pipeline.
- Service accounts that outlive the project that created them.
- People logging in interactively with a machine identity, which hides who actually acted.

blocks.title: Identity classification questions
blocks.md: Shared accounts are almost always the wrong answer. The best answers give **every human, workload and agent its own identity**, with a **named owner**, the **strongest suitable authentication**, and a record in the **inventory**.

q.q: A team runs five customer-service agents, all using one service account created by a developer who has since left. What is the BEST first step?
o: Change the shared service account’s password, and store the new one in the team wiki
Give each agent its own identity with a named owner, then retire the shared account
Leave the setup as it is, because the agents only call internal systems
Move the shared service account into the admin group, so failures are easier to fix
q.why: Distinct identities make each agent’s actions attributable and individually revocable, and an owner keeps them governed. Rotating a shared password keeps the shared account; internal use doesn’t remove the risk; admin rights make it worse.

sections.title: Identity architectures for non-repudiation and accountability

scenes.title: Proving who did what
scenes.say: When an agent issues a refund or deletes a record, you need to prove which identity did it, on whose behalf, and that the record of it hasn’t been altered. | This video covers identity architectures that provide non-repudiation and verified accountability in AI systems.

scenes.title: A chain of accountability
scenes.say: Accountability is a chain, and every link must hold. It starts with a user who signs in with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication. | The AI application holds an authenticated session for that user. | The agent acts with its own identity, plus a delegated token that records the user it is acting for. | The tool or API validates both identities and the token’s scope before doing anything. | It writes a record of who acted, for whom, what was done and when, signed so it can’t be quietly changed. | And the record goes into a tamper-evident log, with each entry chained to the one before.

scenes.title: Impersonation and delegation
rows: Only by locking out the user
scenes.say: There are two ways for an agent to act for a user, and only one supports accountability. | With impersonation, the agent’s token looks exactly like the user’s. With delegation, the token shows both the user and the agent acting for them. | So an impersonation audit trail can’t tell the agent from the person, while a delegation trail records both. | An impersonating agent can do everything the user can. A delegated agent gets only the scopes the task needs. | And to stop an impersonating agent, you have to lock out the user, while a delegated agent can be revoked on its own.

scenes.title: Building blocks of non-repudiation
scenes.say: Non-repudiation rests on six building blocks. | Unique identities: no shared accounts, and no API keys used by several people or agents. | Strong authentication: phishing-resistant MFA for people, and mutual TLS or workload identity for machines. | Proof of possession: tokens bound to a key the holder controls, so a stolen token alone is useless. | Signed actions: high-impact requests and approvals carry digital signatures. | Trusted, synchronised time, so the order of events can be proven. | And protected evidence: tamper-evident logs kept for the required period.

items: Accountability is a chain from user to agent to tool to log
Delegate, don’t impersonate: tokens should show user and agent
Unique identities, strong authentication, bound tokens, signatures
Trusted time and tamper-evident evidence complete the chain
scenes.say: To recap. | Accountability is a chain, running from the user through the agent and the tool to a protected log. | Agents should use delegation, not impersonation, so tokens show both the user and the agent. | Use unique identities, strong authentication, proof-of-possession tokens and signed actions. | And complete the chain with trusted time and tamper-evident evidence.

blocks.md:
### What non-repudiation requires
**Non-repudiation** is assurance that an actor can’t credibly deny an action. It needs four things together: a **strong binding** between the action and a unique identity, **integrity** of the request and the record, **reliable time**, and **protected evidence** that survives long enough to be used. Shared accounts, shared API keys and bearer tokens that anyone can replay all weaken it.

### Delegation in practice
- **OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693)** lets a service swap a user’s token for a new one that records both the subject (the user) and the **actor** (the agent), with narrower scopes and audience. Multi-hop delegation can nest actors, so the full chain is visible.
- **On-behalf-of flows** in identity platforms do the same job: the downstream API sees who the user is and which application or agent is acting.
- **Consent and scope:** users or administrators approve what an agent may do; tokens carry only those scopes and expire with the task.
- **Never share passwords** with an agent, and never let an agent reuse a user’s session cookie. Both are impersonation.

### Binding tokens and signing actions
- **Proof-of-possession tokens:** DPoP (RFC 9449) and mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705) tie a token to a key held by the client, so a stolen token can’t be replayed elsewhere.
- **Signed requests:** HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) or signed payloads let a recipient verify which key sent a request and that it wasn’t altered.
- **Hardware-backed keys:** keep signing keys for workloads and agents in HSMs, TPMs or cloud KMS, so they can’t be copied.
- **Signed approvals:** human approvals of high-impact agent actions should be authenticated and recorded with the approver’s identity, not just a click in a shared console.

### Verified accountability for AI
- Record **what the agent was** when it acted: model version, system prompt version, tools and policy configuration. Behaviour depends on them, so investigations need them.
- Link every agent identity to a **human sponsor**, and every high-impact action to the **user** it served and any **approver**.
- Keep logs **tamper-evident** (hash chains, write-once storage) and **time-synchronised**, and retain them as law and policy require (Module 3.5).
- Make the trail **queryable**: investigators should be able to answer "who did this, for whom, with what authority?" in minutes.

blocks.title: Accountability questions
blocks.md: Choose **delegation over impersonation**, **unique identities over shared ones**, and **bound or signed credentials over plain bearer secrets**. If a scenario says "we can’t tell whether the user or the agent did it", the fix is delegated tokens and logs that record **both** identities.

q.q: An investigation can’t determine whether a customer or the support agent acting for them approved a refund, because the agent used the customer’s session. Which change BEST fixes this for the future?
o: Ask customers to confirm refunds by email, so that there is a written record of each one
Issue the agent delegated tokens that record both identities, and log both on every action
Store the customer’s password securely, so the agent can sign in properly when needed
Give the agent its own administrator account, separate from all customer sessions
q.why: Delegated tokens show the user and the acting agent, so logs can attribute each action and the agent can be scoped and revoked separately. Emails don’t fix attribution, sharing passwords is impersonation, and an admin account gives far too much authority.

scenes.title: Machines proving who they are
scenes.sub: M2M authentication protocols and API tokens
scenes.say: Most traffic in an AI platform is machine to machine: pipelines calling storage, services calling model APIs, agents calling tools. Each call has to prove who is calling. | This video compares the main machine-to-machine authentication options, and how to handle API tokens safely.

scenes.title: Three ways for machines to authenticate
scenes.say: There are three main options. | An API key is a static, shared string. With OAuth client credentials, the client holds a secret or private key and exchanges it for tokens. With workload identity, nothing secret is stored at all: the platform vouches for the workload. | API keys last until someone rotates them. OAuth access tokens are short-lived. Workload identity tokens last minutes to hours and renew automatically. | API keys are often broad, OAuth tokens carry scopes and an audience, and workload identity is bound to the specific workload. | So the main risks are, respectively: leaked and reused keys, a leaked client secret, and a misconfigured trust relationship. Prefer workload identity wherever the platform supports it.

scenes.title: Workload identity federation
scenes.say: Here is how workload identity federation removes stored secrets. A workload, such as a training pipeline, needs to reach a cloud API. | Its own platform, for example a CI system or Kubernetes, issues it a signed, short-lived identity token describing exactly which workload it is. | The workload presents that token to the target cloud’s token service, which checks it against a trust policy: right issuer, right repository or service account, right branch. | If it matches, the workload receives a short-lived access token, scoped to specific permissions and bound to one audience. | The target API validates the token’s signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scope on every call. No long-lived key was ever stored.

scenes.title: API token hygiene

items.h: Keep out of prompts and code

scenes.say: Whatever the mechanism, handle tokens carefully. | Keep lifetimes short: minutes, not months. | Give each token a narrow scope and a single audience. | Where possible, bind tokens to a key, using proof-of-possession or mutual TLS, so a stolen token can’t be replayed. | Keep tokens out of prompts, source code, client apps and logs. | Be able to rotate and revoke quickly, and test that you can. | And monitor use: unusual spend, volume or location can reveal a stolen key.

items: Prefer workload identity; then OAuth; API keys only where unavoidable
Federation swaps platform identity for short-lived, scoped tokens
Validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scope
Short-lived, bound, scoped tokens; never in prompts, code or clients
scenes.say: To recap. | Prefer workload identity, then OAuth client credentials, and use static API keys only where nothing else is possible. | Workload identity federation exchanges a platform-issued identity for short-lived, scoped tokens, with no stored secret. | APIs must validate every token’s signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scope. | And keep tokens short-lived, bound, narrowly scoped, and out of prompts, code and client apps.

blocks.md:
### M2M protocols and patterns
| Mechanism | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **API keys** | A static secret sent with each request | Simple but weak: often broad, long-lived and copied into many places. If unavoidable, scope per project, set spend limits and IP allow-lists, and rotate |
| **OAuth 2.0 client credentials** | A client authenticates to an authorisation server and receives a short-lived access token | Prefer private-key JWT client authentication (RFC 7523) or mTLS over shared client secrets |
| **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** | Both sides present certificates | Strong service-to-service authentication; certificates must be short-lived and rotated automatically |
| **Workload identity federation** | A platform-issued identity token (for example, from a CI system or Kubernetes) is exchanged for cloud credentials under a trust policy | Removes stored secrets; trust policies must be precise (repository, branch, service account) |
| **SPIFFE and SPIRE** | An open standard and runtime that issue short-lived identities (SVIDs, as X.509 certificates or JWTs) to workloads, based on attestation | Portable workload identity across clusters and clouds |
| **Kubernetes service account tokens** | Projected, audience-bound, expiring tokens for pods | Avoid legacy non-expiring tokens |

MCP servers use OAuth 2.1, and must accept only tokens issued for them (Module 4.1).

### Validating tokens
Every API should check a token’s **signature** (with the expected algorithm and a trusted key), **issuer**, **audience**, **expiry** and not-before time, and **scopes**. Reject tokens meant for other services, because accepting them enables confused deputy attacks. Prefer short-lived tokens with server-side revocation for high-risk actions.

### A cautionary case
In 2023, researchers at Wiz found that Microsoft AI researchers had shared open-source training material through a cloud storage link whose token granted **full control of the entire storage account**, with an expiry date decades away. The account held about 38 TB of internal data, including secrets, private keys and internal messages. The lesson: scope tokens to the exact resource and permission, keep lifetimes short, and track every token you issue.

### Model provider API keys
- Keep them **server-side**: never embed them in mobile apps, browsers or desktop clients; route requests through your own backend or AI gateway.
- Use **separate keys per application and environment**, with spending limits and usage alerts.
- Prefer **federated or workload-based access** to cloud-hosted models where the platform offers it.
- Treat a leaked key as an incident: revoke, review usage and cost, find the source (Section 5).

blocks.title: M2M questions
blocks.md: The strongest answer usually **removes the stored secret** (workload identity federation) or makes credentials **short-lived, scoped and bound**. Rotating a long-lived key more often is better than nothing, but rarely the best option.

q.q: A CI pipeline deploys models to a cloud account using a long-lived access key stored in the CI system’s settings. Which change BEST reduces the risk of credential theft?
o: Rotate the access key every 30 days, and limit who can view the CI settings
Use workload identity federation, so the pipeline receives short-lived, scoped credentials
Encrypt the stored access key with the CI system’s built-in secret masking feature
Copy the access key into each individual pipeline job, so that no single place holds all of it
q.why: Federation replaces the stored key with short-lived credentials issued only to the verified pipeline, so there is nothing long-lived to steal. Rotation and masking still leave a powerful static key, and copying it spreads the risk.

sections.title: Federated identity, MFA and single sign-on for AI

scenes.title: One identity, many AI tools
scenes.sub: Federation, single sign-on and multi-factor authentication
scenes.say: Staff now use dozens of AI tools and platforms. A separate password for each would be a security and governance nightmare, and leavers would keep access for months. | This video covers federated identity, single sign-on and multi-factor authentication for AI platforms and tools.

scenes.title: Single sign-on through federation
scenes.say: Here is single sign-on through federation. A user opens an AI tool. | Instead of a local password, the tool sends them to the organisation’s identity provider, which enforces multi-factor authentication and conditional access checks, such as device health and location. | The identity provider returns a signed assertion, using SAML or OpenID Connect. | The AI application trusts that assertion and starts a session, without ever seeing a password. | Alongside it, SCIM provisioning creates, updates and removes accounts in the tool automatically. | So when someone leaves, disabling them once in the identity provider removes their access everywhere.

scenes.title: SAML and OpenID Connect
scenes.say: Two federation protocols dominate. | SAML uses signed XML assertions. OpenID Connect uses JSON web tokens. | SAML is a standalone XML standard. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0, which on its own handles authorisation, not authentication. | SAML remains common for enterprise web single sign-on. OpenID Connect suits modern web, mobile and API scenarios, and most new AI platforms support it.

scenes.title: MFA that resists phishing

items.d: Re-verify at the moment of risk

scenes.say: Not all multi-factor authentication is equal. | Passkeys and other FIDO2 authenticators are phishing-resistant by design, because they only work on the genuine site. | Smart cards and certificate-based methods are also strong. | If you use push notifications, require number matching, which defeats approval-fatigue attacks. | Avoid SMS and voice codes for administrators, because they can be intercepted or hijacked through SIM swaps. | Apply conditional access based on device, location and risk. | And require step-up authentication for sensitive AI actions, such as approving an agent’s payment or exporting model weights.

scenes.title: Federation for AI-specific cases
scenes.say: Federation matters in five AI-specific places. | AI software-as-a-service tools should accept only corporate single sign-on, and block personal accounts, which also reduces shadow AI. | Model platform and cloud AI consoles need strong MFA and just-in-time administrative access. | Notebooks and developer tools should use single sign-on with short sessions. | Agents acting for users should get delegated OAuth tokens with consent, never a user’s password. | And partners should sign in through federation with their own identity provider, rather than with local accounts you have to remember to remove.

items: Federate AI tools to one identity provider; provision with SCIM
SAML for enterprise web SSO; OIDC for modern apps and APIs
Phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access and step-up
SSO-only AI SaaS; delegated OAuth for agents; federate partners
scenes.say: To recap. | Federate every AI tool to one identity provider, and provision and deprovision accounts with SCIM. | SAML suits enterprise web single sign-on; OpenID Connect suits modern apps and APIs. | Use phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, and step-up authentication for sensitive actions. | And enforce single sign-on for AI services, delegated OAuth for agents, and federation for partners.

blocks.md:
### Federation concepts
- **Identity provider (IdP):** authenticates users and issues assertions or tokens; enforces MFA and conditional access.
- **Service provider or relying party:** the application that trusts the IdP, such as an AI SaaS tool or model platform console.
- **SAML 2.0:** XML-based, widely used for enterprise web SSO.
- **OpenID Connect (OIDC):** an identity layer on OAuth 2.0, issuing ID tokens (JWTs); suited to web, mobile, APIs and single-page apps.
- **OAuth 2.0:** delegated *authorisation*, not authentication. Using an OAuth access token as proof of identity is a classic design error.
- **SCIM:** a standard API for provisioning and deprovisioning accounts and groups in connected applications.
- **Just-in-time provisioning:** creating an account at first login from the assertion; pair it with SCIM or regular reviews so accounts are also removed.

### MFA strength
NIST SP 800-63B defines authenticator assurance levels: higher levels require stronger, phishing-resistant authenticators, and SMS-based codes are restricted. CISA and other agencies recommend **phishing-resistant MFA** (FIDO2 passkeys or PKI-based smart cards) for privileged users and high-value systems. Push approval alone is vulnerable to **MFA fatigue**: in the 2022 Uber breach, an attacker repeatedly sent push requests and contacted the employee posing as IT support until a request was approved. Number matching and phishing-resistant methods counter this.

### AI-specific practice
- **Enforce SSO for AI services**, including enterprise tiers of public chatbots, and use domain controls to stop staff signing up with corporate email on personal plans (Module 2.6 covers shadow AI).
- **Privileged AI access:** consoles for model platforms, vector databases and training clusters need phishing-resistant MFA, just-in-time elevation and session recording for administrators (Module 4.6).
- **Session management:** short session lifetimes for high-risk tools, re-authentication for sensitive actions, and revocation when risk changes.
- **Agents:** use delegated OAuth flows with explicit consent and scoped tokens (Section 2); never store or share user passwords with an agent.
- **Customers:** offer passkeys and MFA for customer-facing AI services that act on accounts or payments.
- **Partners:** federate with partner identity providers, with attribute mapping and access reviews, rather than creating local accounts.

blocks.title: Federation and MFA questions
blocks.md: Prefer **centralised SSO with SCIM deprovisioning** over local accounts, **phishing-resistant MFA** over SMS or plain push, and **step-up authentication** for high-risk actions. Remember that **OAuth is for authorisation**; OpenID Connect adds authentication.

q.q: An audit finds that 40 former employees still have active accounts on an AI writing platform, because accounts there are created and removed by hand. What is the BEST fix?
o: Ask managers to email IT whenever someone leaves, so the account can be removed
Federate the platform to the corporate IdP with SSO, and provision accounts through SCIM
Reset every account’s password each quarter, so that former employees are unable to sign in
Disable the platform’s accounts once a year during the annual access review
q.why: Federation means disabling a user in the IdP blocks sign-in everywhere, and SCIM removes the account in the platform automatically. Manual emails and annual reviews are slow and error-prone, and password resets don’t remove access.

sections.title: Secrets and key management for AI platforms

blocks.title: Keeping secrets out of the conversation

scenes.title: Keeping secrets out of the conversation
scenes.sub: Secrets and key management for AI platforms
scenes.say: AI platforms run on secrets: model provider keys, database credentials, signing keys and tool tokens. They also create new places for secrets to leak, such as prompts, notebooks, agent configurations and logs. | This video covers secrets and key management for AI platforms.

scenes.title: Where AI secrets leak

items.d: Models can be talked into revealing them
Keys pasted into cells and outputs

scenes.say: AI platforms leak secrets in new places. | In prompts and system prompts, where a model can often be talked into repeating them. | In notebooks and experiment tracking, where keys get pasted into cells and saved in outputs. | In agent and MCP configuration files, which often hold tokens in plain text. | In training data: secrets in scraped code or documents can be memorised by a model and reproduced later. | In logs and traces, because prompt logging captures whatever users paste. | And in client apps, where a model API key embedded in a mobile app is effectively given to every user.

scenes.title: A secrets architecture for AI

layers.label: Central vault, backed by hardware
layers.sub: One governed home for every secret

layers.label: Workload identity to reach it
layers.sub: No secret needed to get the secrets

layers.label: Runtime, server-side injection
layers.sub: Never in images, code or prompts

layers.label: Brokered access for agents
layers.sub: The model never sees the credential

scenes.say: A sound secrets architecture for AI has six layers. | A central vault, backed by hardware security modules, as the one governed home for every secret. | Workloads reach the vault using workload identity, so no secret is needed to fetch the secrets. | Secrets are injected at runtime, on the server side, and never baked into images, code or prompts. | Agents get brokered access: a tool gateway attaches the credential to the outgoing call, so the model never sees it. | Secrets are short-lived and, where possible, generated dynamically for each task or session. | And everything is scanned and monitored, so leaks are found quickly and unusual use is spotted.

scenes.title: Brokered credentials for agents
scenes.say: Here is credential brokering in action. The agent decides it needs to call an external service, and asks for the action through a tool call. | A tool gateway checks the request against policy: is this agent allowed this action, with these arguments, right now? | If so, the gateway obtains a short-lived credential from the vault. | The gateway, not the agent, makes the call to the external API with that credential. | And only the result goes back to the agent. The secret never enters the model’s context, so no prompt injection can make the model reveal it.

scenes.title: When an AI key leaks

items.d: What was called, what was read

scenes.say: When a model API key or other AI credential leaks, act in order. | Revoke it and issue a replacement immediately, before investigating, because automated scanners find exposed keys within minutes. | Review usage and cost: what was called, what data was read, and how much was spent. | Find the source: a repository, a prompt, a log, a notebook or an app. | Purge the copies from history, logs and any datasets that might be used for training. | And prevent a repeat with secret scanning, credential brokering and short-lived credentials.

items: AI adds leak paths: prompts, notebooks, configs, training data, logs, apps
Vault plus workload identity; inject at runtime, server-side
Broker credentials so models never see them
Short-lived secrets, scanning, monitoring and a fast revoke playbook
scenes.say: To recap. | AI platforms add new leak paths: prompts, notebooks, agent configurations, training data, logs and client apps. | Keep secrets in a hardware-backed vault, reach it with workload identity, and inject secrets at runtime on the server side. | Broker credentials for agents, so models never see them. | And use short-lived secrets, continuous scanning and monitoring, and a tested playbook for revoking leaked keys.

blocks.md:
### Secrets in AI platforms
| Secret | Examples | Key practices |
|---|---|---|
| **Model provider keys** | Keys for hosted LLM APIs | Server-side only; per app and environment; spend limits; usage alerts |
| **Cloud and data credentials** | Storage, warehouse, vector database access | Workload identity; dynamic, short-lived database credentials |
| **Tool and connector tokens** | MCP servers, SaaS APIs, webhooks | Brokered through a gateway; scoped OAuth tokens; never in tool descriptions |
| **Signing keys** | Model signing (Module 3.6), container signing, request signing | HSM or KMS; separation of duties; keyless signing where suitable |
| **Encryption keys** | Data and weight encryption (Module 3.4) | KMS or HSM; customer-managed keys; rotation and destruction |
| **Watermark and fingerprint keys** | Ownership verification (Module 3.6) | Restricted access; trusted verification only |

### Principles
- **Eliminate first:** replace static secrets with workload identity and federation wherever possible (Section 3).
- **Centralise:** one vault or KMS, with access policies, audit logs and hardware protection for high-value keys (Module 3.4 covers the key lifecycle).
- **Never put secrets in prompts or model context.** System prompts can leak (OWASP LLM07), and anything in the context can be repeated by the model.
- **Broker credentials for agents:** the tool layer attaches credentials to outbound calls; the model only sees results.
- **Keep secrets server-side:** client apps go through your backend or AI gateway.
- **Short-lived and dynamic:** issue credentials per task or session, and revoke them when it ends.
- **Scan everywhere:** pre-commit hooks and push protection; CI pipelines; notebooks and experiment trackers; prompt and trace logs; and **datasets before training**. In 2025, researchers at Truffle Security reported finding nearly 12,000 live API keys and passwords in a single snapshot of Common Crawl, a web dataset widely used for training language models.
- **Monitor:** provider usage dashboards, spend alerts and anomaly detection on credential use.
- **Rehearse revocation:** a tested playbook to revoke and replace any secret quickly, including those embedded in partners’ systems.

### Common anti-patterns
- An agent configuration file with a provider key in plain text, committed to a repository.
- A "temporary" key in a notebook that ends up in a shared experiment log.
- A system prompt containing a database connection string "so the model can query it".
- The same model API key used by every team, with no way to attribute or limit use.

blocks.title: Secrets questions
blocks.md: If a secret appears in a **prompt, a client app, a notebook or a repository**, the best answer moves it **server-side into a vault**, ideally replaced by **workload identity** or **brokered** short-lived credentials. After a leak, **revoke first**, then investigate.

q.q: A developer gives an agent a database password by including it in the agent’s system prompt, so it can run queries. What is the BEST alternative?
o: Encode the password in base64 inside the prompt, so the model can’t read it directly
Have a tool gateway run the queries with vault-issued credentials the model never sees
Tell the model in the prompt never to reveal the password to any user, under any circumstances
Use a longer, more complex password, so that it is much harder for attackers to guess
q.why: Brokering keeps credentials out of the model’s context, so no injection or leak of the prompt can expose them, and the gateway can enforce policy on each query. Encoding isn’t protection, prompt instructions can be overridden, and password strength doesn’t help once it is disclosed.

quiz.q: Why should each AI agent have its own identity rather than share a service account?
o: Shared accounts are more expensive to license from most identity providers
Its actions can be attributed to it, and it can be revoked without affecting others
Agents run faster when each one authenticates with a different account name
Identity providers refuse to issue any tokens to accounts that are used by more than one agent
quiz.why: Distinct identities make actions attributable and let one agent be scoped, monitored or revoked on its own.

quiz.q: What is the MOST common weakness of non-human identities?
o: They are phished through convincing emails more often than people are
Long-lived secrets and excessive privileges, often with no clear owner
They can’t be given any multi-factor authentication of any kind
They expire too quickly for automated pipelines and services to use
quiz.why: Machine identities tend to accumulate broad rights and static secrets, and outlive the projects and people that created them.

quiz.q: What does a delegated token give that impersonation doesn’t?
o: Access to more data than the user has, which improves the quality of the agent’s answers
A record of both the user and the agent acting for them, with narrower scope
A permanent session, so the agent never needs to re-authenticate
The user’s password, so the agent can sign in to any system as them
quiz.why: Delegation (for example, token exchange with an actor claim) shows who acted for whom, limits the agent to the task, and lets it be revoked separately.

quiz.q: Why do proof-of-possession tokens strengthen accountability?
o: They last longer than bearer tokens, so there are fewer gaps in the logs
They are bound to a key the holder controls, so a stolen token can’t be replayed
They contain the user’s password, which proves who made the request
They can be shared safely between several different agents that are working on the same task
quiz.why: Binding a token to a key (DPoP or mTLS) means only the legitimate holder can use it, which makes actions harder to fake and easier to attribute.

quiz.q: Which M2M approach removes the need to store a long-lived secret at all?
o: A static API key kept in an encrypted environment variable on every server that uses it
Workload identity federation, exchanging platform identity for short-lived tokens
OAuth client credentials using a shared client secret in configuration
Basic authentication with a long, randomly generated password
quiz.why: Federation relies on the platform vouching for the workload, so there is no stored key to steal or rotate.

quiz.q: Which checks should an API perform on every access token it receives?
o: Only that the token is present and long enough to be genuine
Its signature, issuer, audience, expiry and the scopes it grants
That the token was issued within the last calendar year
That the token’s format matches the one used in the documentation
quiz.why: Full validation stops forged, expired, over-scoped and misdirected tokens, including tokens issued for other services.

quiz.q: Where should a mobile app’s calls to a hosted LLM get their provider API key?
o: From the app bundle, encrypted with a key that is also stored inside the app
Nowhere: the app calls the organisation’s backend, which holds the key
From the user, who pastes their own key into the app’s settings screen
From a public configuration file that the app downloads at start-up
quiz.why: Any key shipped in a client can be extracted by users. A backend or AI gateway keeps the key server-side and enforces limits.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN security benefit of SCIM provisioning for AI tools?
o: It encrypts all of the prompts that are sent from the identity provider to each AI tool
Accounts are created and removed automatically, so leavers lose access promptly
It replaces the need for any multi-factor authentication on the tools
It lets users choose their own passwords for each tool they use
quiz.why: Automated provisioning and deprovisioning closes the gap where former staff keep accounts on tools that were managed by hand.

quiz.q: Which MFA method is phishing-resistant by design?
o: One-time codes sent to the user’s phone by SMS text message
Passkeys and other FIDO2 hardware-backed authenticators
Push notifications that the user simply approves or denies
Security questions about the user’s first school or pet
quiz.why: FIDO2 authenticators are bound to the genuine site’s origin, so credentials can’t be relayed through a fake site.

quiz.q: What does credential brokering for agents achieve?
o: The agent stores credentials more securely in its long-term memory
The tool layer attaches credentials to calls, so the model never sees them
Credentials are shared between agents, so fewer have to be issued
The agent can create brand-new credentials for itself whenever it decides that it needs them
quiz.why: Keeping secrets out of the model’s context means no prompt injection or prompt leak can expose them.

quiz.q: A model provider API key is found in a public repository. What should happen FIRST?
o: Investigate how long the key was public before deciding on any action
Revoke the key and issue a replacement, then review usage and find the source
Delete the file from the repository, which removes the exposure entirely
Email the provider to ask whether anyone has used the key since it leaked
quiz.why: Automated scanners find exposed keys within minutes, so revocation comes first. Deleting the file leaves the key in history and copies.

quiz.q: Why should training datasets be scanned for secrets before use?
o: Secrets make datasets too large to process efficiently on GPUs
Models can memorise secrets in training data and reproduce them later
Data protection law requires every dataset to be free of passwords
Secrets change the tokenizer, which reduces the model’s accuracy
quiz.why: Memorised credentials can be extracted from a model, so scrub secrets from code, documents and crawls before training.

exam.q: An identity review finds 3,000 service accounts and API keys across the AI platform. About 40% have no identifiable owner, and many have administrator rights. What should the identity team do FIRST?
o: Delete every unowned account immediately, whatever pipelines might break as a result
Discover and classify them, assign owners, and prioritise unowned privileged identities for review
Reset the passwords and keys of all 3,000 accounts, and email the new ones to the platform team
Commission a new identity platform, and leave the current accounts in place until it is ready
exam.why: You can’t govern what you haven’t classified or assigned. Ownership and risk-based prioritisation let the team reduce the riskiest identities first without breaking critical services. Mass deletion is reckless, mass resets spread secrets, and waiting leaves the risk in place.

exam.q: A bank’s customer-support agent can issue refunds. Regulators require proof of who authorised each refund. Today the agent uses one service account for every customer. Which design BEST meets the requirement?
o: Keep the service account, but add each customer’s name to the refund description field
Delegated tokens recording customer and agent, step-up approval for refunds, and tamper-evident logs
Give the agent each customer’s online banking password, so that every refund comes from their own account
Ask a supervisor to approve every refund verbally, and note the approval in a spreadsheet
exam.why: Delegation ties each action to both the customer and the agent, step-up authentication captures the authorisation strongly, and tamper-evident logs preserve the evidence. Free-text names, shared passwords and spreadsheets don’t provide non-repudiation.

exam.q: An investigation into a data deletion by an AI agent can’t determine which model version and instructions the agent was running at the time. What should be added to the audit design?
o: Nothing, because the agent’s identity alone is enough to attribute the action
Record the model version, system prompt version and tool configuration with each action
Require the agent to explain each action in plain language, and store its explanations
Keep screenshots of the agent’s user interface for every session it handles
exam.why: An agent’s behaviour depends on its model, prompt and tools, so accountability requires recording the configuration in force when it acted. Self-explanations can be wrong, and screenshots don’t capture configuration.

exam.q: Several internal services call a model inference API using one shared API key that hasn’t been rotated in two years. Which approach BEST improves authentication?
o: Rotate the shared key every month, and announce each new key to teams by email
Give each service its own workload identity, with short-lived, audience-bound tokens
Move the shared key into an environment variable on every server that needs it
Allow the API to be called only during business hours, to limit when misuse could occur
exam.why: Per-service workload identity makes calls attributable, removes the long-lived shared secret, and limits each token to the inference API. Rotation by email still shares one key, environment variables don’t change its nature, and time windows don’t authenticate.

exam.q: Staff are signing up for a popular AI chatbot with their corporate email addresses on personal plans. Security wants control without banning AI. What is the BEST approach?
o: Block the chatbot’s domain at the firewall, and remind all staff of the acceptable use policy for AI
Adopt the enterprise tier with SSO and SCIM, claim the corporate domain, and route staff to it
Ask staff to add their personal accounts to a register kept by the security team
Allow personal plans, but require staff to delete their chat history every week
exam.why: An enterprise tier federated to the IdP brings accounts under corporate MFA, provisioning and data terms, and domain controls stop unmanaged personal sign-ups, while still letting staff use AI. Blocking pushes usage elsewhere, and registers or deletion rules aren’t enforceable controls.

exam.q: An attacker phished an ML engineer’s password and one-time SMS code, then signed in to the model platform console and downloaded weights. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Requiring the engineer to change their password every 30 days
Phishing-resistant MFA, such as passkeys, with step-up for weight exports
Sending SMS codes to two different phone numbers instead of one
Adding a prominent warning banner to the console about the value of the model weights
exam.why: FIDO2 passkeys can’t be relayed through a phishing site, and step-up authentication for high-risk actions adds a further barrier. Password rotation, extra SMS codes and banners don’t stop real-time phishing.

exam.q: A team’s MCP server configuration file contains plain-text tokens for five SaaS tools, and is shared across developer laptops. Which change BEST reduces the risk?
o: Encrypt the file with a single strong password that all of the developers share between them
Run tools behind a gateway that injects short-lived, vault-issued tokens per call
Store the file in a private repository, so only the team can read it
Rename the tokens in the file so that attackers won’t recognise them
exam.why: Brokered, short-lived credentials from a vault remove standing secrets from laptops and configuration, and the gateway can enforce policy. A shared password, a private repository and renaming all leave long-lived tokens exposed.
